records.name: Bahia
records.current_summary: Bahia recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — among the highest state tallies of that year's 80, on the largest population among the upper-ranked states (SBT News, 26 January 2026; Valor Internacional). No Bahia-specific ordinance or statutory restriction was identified; federal law applies uniformly across Brazil.  The documented picture is a high absolute toll diluted by size rather than eliminated by it: the dossiers place the state inside the Northeastern region that accounts for the bulk of national killings, with the consistent victim profile (97% travestis and trans women, majority aged 18–29, 70% Black among racially identified cases, most killings outside state capitals) describing who carries the risk. For a visibly trans visitor the operative fact is persistence — Bahia appears in the top ranked band of consecutive annual dossiers — not any local legal regime.

sources.claim: SBT News (26 Jan 2026): ANTRA 2025 dossier — Bahia recorded 7 trans killings in 2025, second tier behind the 8-count states; among 1,261 killings 2017-2025 Bahia is 3rd with 97 (São Paulo 151, Ceará 107). Supports the record's tally.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (404; the date segment in the seed URL is dash-separated and does not resolve); the dossier cites this Valor Internacional report (27 Jan 2026) as a second source for the 2025 state-level killing counts behind the Ceará/Minas Gerais pair.

G1 Bahia, Dec. 9, 2025: police are investigating as feminicide the killing of Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of Bahia, on the weekend of Dec. 6-7. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station himself and was released after confessing and claiming self-defence; the Civil Police confirmed the feminicide investigation. For this record: a documented killing in Bahia framed by the state police as gender-based (feminicide) with the suspect initially released.

G1 Bahia, Jan. 27, 2023: the ANTRA dossier ranked Bahia the seventh Brazilian state most killing trans people, with 7 killings of travestis in the state in 2022, and recapped emblematic cases; Pernambuco led that year's negative ranking nationally. For this record: documents Bahia's appearance in the top-ranked band of consecutive annual dossiers, grounding the summary's persistence finding across years.

records.name: Maranhao
records.current_summary: Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — the same count the association dossier logged for it in 2024 — so its position in the ranking's middle-upper band is persistent rather than a one-year spike (SBT News, 26 January 2026; CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025). No Maranhão-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people is documented in the audited sources; federal law applies uniformly.  The national profile the dossiers attach to this state's region — victims young, Black, poor and Northeastern; 97% travestis and trans women; most killings in public places, at night, and outside state capitals where monitoring and policy access are thinner — maps onto Maranhão's place in both tables. The documented risk is structural exposure: two consecutive years of above-median lethal counts in a country that leads the world's tallies, without any local legal change either way.

sources.claim: SBT News (26 Jan 2026) reports ANTRA's 9th annual dossier: 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil in 2025, a ~34% fall year-on-year, Brazil first in world rankings; victims overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. National dossier — the table behind this record's 2025 state count. Supplies this record's 2025 count (5 of 80).

CNN Brasil (27 Jan 2025) on ANTRA's 2024 dossier: Brazil led world trans-killings rankings for a 16th consecutive year with 122 killed in 2024 (16% below 2023); victims mostly young, Black women, many from the Northeast; crimes marked by extreme violence. Source behind this record's 2024 count and its year-over-year comparison.

records.name: Para
records.current_summary: Pará recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, in the middle band of the ANTRA dossier's state ranking of that year's 80 national killings (SBT News, 26 January 2026). No Pará-specific statute, ordinance or policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources; the federal framework applies uniformly. The second audited source lists the 2024 worst-hit states without naming this state, so its 2024 position cannot be fixed from the record.  What the dossiers do document bears directly on a vast Amazonian state: roughly two-thirds to 68% of such killings nationally occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and victims are overwhelmingly young Black travestis and trans women killed in public places. For a trans visitor travelling beyond the main metropolitan area, the least-monitored geography is precisely where the recorded killings sit.

records.name: Alagoas
records.current_summary: Alagoas recorded 6 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024 — among the elevated small-state totals in that year's ANTRA dossier table (CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025) — and 2 in 2025 (SBT News, 26 January 2026). No Alagoas-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding is documented; federal law applies uniformly.  The swing between consecutive dossiers on a small population is itself the finding: at these denominators a couple of cases moves a state's position sharply, which is why the monitoring body cautions that falling national counts reflect violence shifting into attempted homicides and persistent under-recording (misclassification of victims' gender identity degrades the data) rather than improving safety. The victim profile the dossiers attach to this region — young, Black, poor, Northeastern, killed in public places at night — places risk wherever a visibly trans person is in public, in a state inside the country's hardest-hit region.

records.name: Sachsen
records.current_summary: Two documented 2025 features raise Sachsen above the German norm for visitor risk around queer visibility: neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest intended to disrupt Dresden's pride march on 31 May 2025 (the march proceeded); and the state government, with two neighbouring states, co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after an abuse-of-self-ID court case ('Fall Liebich'), alleging misuse of the self-ID right — an organised, multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law.  Germany's national protections and functioning rule of law apply unchanged here; the documented counter-action was policed without event cancellation or reported injuries. Earlier assertions of a wider multi-city attack pattern (Bautzen mob sizes, Döbeln prosecutions) lack support in the retained sources and are removed from the record.

records.name: Bauchi
records.current_summary: Bauchi sits in the twelve-state Sharia criminal bloc of northern Nigeria, and it is where that system's ultimate penalty was actually pronounced: in June 2022 a Sharia court in Ningi sentenced three men — including a 70-year-old — to death by stoning for same-sex acts after arrest by the Hisbah religious police, reportedly the first time a death sentence has actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out; no execution is on record.  The appellate counterweight is real but fragile: the state's Upper Sharia Court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003 (denial of counsel, defective confession), and Amnesty International recorded a string of similar successful appeals. A June 2025 country-of-origin note confirms the code remains in force, and corporal enforcement of Sharia morality law in Bauchi continues to be cited in 2025–26 advisory material.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (Reuters returns 401 to automated fetches); the underlying Reuters report (2 July 2022) covers the Ningi Sharia court sentencing three men - a 70-year-old among them - to death by stoning for homosexuality after a 14 June 2022 Hisbah arrest, the first time the death penalty has actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria.

Amnesty International press release (2004): the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning 'sodomy' sentence (convicted 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001) for denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003 - 'a number of cases where convictions and sentences to death have been quashed on appeal'. Also records a then-pending stoning appeal (Usman/Ibrahim) before a Sharia Court of Appeal in Niger State.

UK Home Office country policy and information note, June 2025, confirming the Sharia Penal Codes of the twelve northern states, including Bauchi, remain in force. The note records that a Sharia court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning for 'homosexual acts' in 2022 but that the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and that a further report placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in Bauchi in May 2024. It also records that at a sodomy trial in January 2014 at Bauchi's Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court an angry mob stormed the premises demanding a death sentence. This is the June 2025 government note the record cites for the code remaining in force and for the 2022 sentence having been pronounced but not executed.

THISDAY, 3 July 2022: a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area of Bauchi State sentenced three men to death by stoning for homosexuality, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna, based on Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested committing the offence at Gwada village, Ningi LGA on 14 June 2022. Second national Nigerian paper confirming that Bauchi's Sharia court actually pronounced the stoning sentence this record is about.

Punch report of the 28 June 2022 Ningi Sharia Court death-by-stoning sentence against three men in Bauchi State, built on interviews with relatives, published 16 July 2022. It records that presiding Shariah judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi held the men violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001, that a 30-day appeal window was granted, and - through relatives of the convicted men - that the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. Confirms both the pronouncement of the sentence and the absence of any execution on record that the summary relies on.

records.name: Kano
records.current_summary: Kano is one of twelve northern Nigerian states running a parallel Sharia criminal code for Muslims: its Penal Code Law took effect 26 November 2000, prescribing 100 lashes plus up to a year's imprisonment for unmarried persons convicted of consensual same-sex activity and stoning to death for married or previously-married offenders. The state's Hisbah religious police are documented as the most active command among the three states studied in a 2019 rights-monitoring survey of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 — enforcement that operates alongside, not merely on paper beside, the secular police.  A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the Sharia codes remain in force and singles out Kano as one of only two states whose law carries a capital maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men. No trans-specific incident is on the state's record; the capital text plus the most active morality-police infrastructure is the finding.

sources.claim: Equaldex log entry #14124: the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000 took effect in Kano on 26 November 2000; consensual same-sex activity draws 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment if unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) if the offender is or has been married.

NOTE: document not retrievable at fetch time (403); the underlying USCIRF 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation uses 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara, and records Hisbah (religious police) activity in each, including Kano as the most active command.

UK Home Office country policy and information note, June 2025, which singles out Kano among the twelve northern Sharia-code states. Its comparative table lists the Kano Sharia Penal Code (2000) as prescribing death by stoning for married or previously married men and 100 lashes with imprisonment for up to one year for unmarried men, and states that in Kano and Katsina the maximum penalty for 'lesbianism' is death while the other ten states punish it by flogging and up to six months' imprisonment. The note also records Kano-specific enforcement and gender-expression facts: eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on the premises of the hisbah in Kano state in 2023, and Kano's separate Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men. This is the June 2025 government note the record cites for the codes remaining in force and for Kano's capital maximum applying to same-sex acts between women as well as men.

records.name: Sokoto
records.current_summary: Sokoto's Sharia Penal Code took effect 31 January 2001 within Nigeria's twelve-state religious-criminal bloc: male same-sex activity draws stoning to death for married or previously-married offenders and 100 lashes for the unmarried, and acts between women are punished by discretionary sentence of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases (2017) covers Sokoto among the three sample states, confirming operational religious courts and Hisbah activity there, and a June 2025 government note confirms the codes remain in force.  No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Sokoto — that record belongs to a neighbouring state — and no trans-specific incident is documented. The finding is capital-heavy statutory text combined with verified court-level enforcement.

sources.claim: Equaldex log entry #14118: the Sharia Penal Code Laws took effect in Sokoto on 31 January 2001; male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and 100 lashes otherwise; sexual acts between women (wsafa) draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment.

This chapter of the academic sourcebook reproduces the full record of a capital prosecution in Sokoto State's Sharia courts. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa (Sokoto State) convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. On her appeal, filed 26 October 2001, the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. For this record the document evidences that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the same capital-punishment framework (for zina, not same-sex conduct) the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

Primary committee reports mapping Sokoto's Sharia adoption: the interim report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999 and the final report on 16 December 1999, with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts applying Sharia law in Sokoto State. They document the state-level groundwork for the Sokoto Sharia Penal Code - in force from 31 January 2001 per this record's other sources - that carries the stoning and lashing penalties for men's same-sex acts described in this record.

flags: ta'azir discretionary punishment (up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment) — precision not carried by any audited source

records.name: Yobe
records.current_summary: Yobe is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states that extended religious law into criminal jurisdiction during the 1999–2002 wave, giving Sharia courts authority over Muslims for conduct beyond the federal criminal code. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the Sharia penal codes in these states — Yobe among them — remain in force, with the death penalty as the maximum for men's same-sex acts across all twelve and penalties for women ranging up to death in a minority of states; the same note's enforcement section records the 2023 public flogging of a person for cross-dressing, a trans-adjacent Sharia-police punishment.  Yobe's own dossier records no state-level court-case study and no further named incidents; the risk profile is the parallel criminal jurisdiction itself plus bloc-wide enforcement reporting, set against federal law that reaches only men's acts.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the twelve states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002 — the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on SOGIESC in Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025): the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct (up to 14 years, attempted 3 years) and is silent on women; Sharia penal codes in the 12 northern states apply to Muslims, with death the maximum for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death (in a minority of states) to flogging and imprisonment; the enforcement-and-Hisbah section records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023 and notes few secular cases reach court.

Reference article on Yobe State recording that the state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims and that Sharia law was established in the state in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim. For this record it confirms, in a jurisdiction-specific source, that Yobe adopted Sharia within the 1999-2002 wave that created the state's parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims.

records.name: Zamfara
records.current_summary: Zamfara is where Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave began: its governor introduced the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 eleven more northern states followed — a parallel system of Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, which the 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms is still operative and capital-punishment-capable for same-sex acts. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 uses Zamfara as one of three sample states, confirming the courts function in practice, not just on paper.  No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Zamfara, and no trans-specific incident appears in the dossier; the finding is pioneering the bloc's enforcement architecture and hosting functioning religious courts.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

Primary state-authored account of Zamfara's Sharia adoption, written by Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Zamfara State, and presented at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. It details Zamfara's enabling legislation - the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999 under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution - which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code, and records the Grand Kadi taking over court administration from 29 June 2000 alongside policy moves against prostitution and gambling. For this record it documents from inside the state government the adoption process that began Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave in Zamfara.

Academic reconstruction of how Zamfara's Sharia Penal Code was made: the Zamfara governor appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementing Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law, and by the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia. The chapter analyses the codification of offences and punishments and the penal-code architecture the Sharia courts of the twelve states apply, grounding this record's claim that Zamfara pioneered the bloc's religious-criminal framework.
